title: Neyman-Pearson Classification under Both Null and Alternative Distributions Shift
claim: Target and source optimal classifiers differ when the null shifts, so the target's confidence region can exclude uninformative sources.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right 1-D axis, dashed threshold lines, bracket below
description: A single horizontal axis carries four bell curves, all Gaussian with the same variance and different means. From left to right: a green curve labeled mu_{0,S1}, a red curve labeled mu_{0,T}, a black curve labeled mu_{0,S2}, and a red curve at the far right labeled mu_{1,T} = mu_{1,S}. Three vertical dashed lines mark the optimal NP thresholds. A dark green line is h*_{S1,alpha}, a red line is h*_{T,alpha}, and a black line is h*_{S2,alpha}. A red square bracket under the axis spans the region between h*_{T,alpha} and h*_{S2,alpha}. It is labeled with the hat-H*_{alpha,T} confidence set. Colors tie each curve to its source or target. The eye goes first to the curves, then to the dashed thresholds and the bracket.
caption: In this figure, we consider one target and two sources that all share the distribution µ1, while µ0 differs across them. All distributions are Gaussian with the same variance but different means. The optimal NP classifiers are denoted by h∗
abstract: We consider the problem of transfer learning in Neyman-Pearson classification, where the objective is to minimize the error w.r.t. a distribution $Î¼_1$, subject to the constraint that the error w.r.t. a distribution $Î¼_0$ remains below a prescribed threshold. While transfer learning has been extensively studied in traditional classification, transfer learning in imbalanced classification such as Neyman-Pearson classification has received much less attention. This setting poses unique challenges, as both types of errors must be simultaneously controlled. Existing works address only the case of distribution shift in $Î¼_1$, whereas in many practical scenarios shifts may occur in both $Î¼_0$ and $Î¼_1$. We derive an adaptive procedure that not only guarantees improved Type-I and Type-II errors when the source is informative, but also automatically adapt to situations where the source is uninformative, thereby avoiding negative transfer. In addition to such statistical guarantees, the procedures is efficient, as shown via complementary computational guarantees.
